paragraphs: I have just examined how the equality of conditions changes the relations among the members of the community in democratic nations, and among the Americans in particular. Now I want to look deeper, at the closer ties of kindred. My purpose here is not to find new truths, but to show how facts already known connect with my subject.

It has been widely remarked that in our time the members of a family stand on an entirely new footing with one another. The distance that once separated a father from his sons has shrunk, and paternal authority, if not destroyed, is at least weakened. Something similar, but even more striking, can be seen in the United States. In America the family, in the Roman and aristocratic sense of the word, does not exist. Only a few traces of it remain in the first years of childhood, when the father exercises, without opposition, the absolute domestic authority that his children’s helplessness makes necessary, and that both their interest and his own undeniable superiority justify. But as soon as the young American nears manhood, the bonds of filial obedience loosen day by day. Master of his thoughts, he soon becomes master of his conduct. Strictly speaking, America has no adolescence: when boyhood ends, the man appears and begins to mark out his own path. It would be a mistake to imagine that a domestic struggle comes first, in which the son wins by a kind of moral violence the liberty his father denied him. The same habits and the same principles that drive the one to assert his independence dispose the other to regard the use of that independence as an undeniable right. The son shows none of the rancorous or unruly passions that trouble men long after they have thrown off an established authority; the father feels none of the bitter, angry regret that tends to outlast a vanished power. The father foresees the limits of his authority long in advance, and when the time comes he gives it up without a fight. The son looks ahead to the exact moment when he will be his own master, and he enters into his freedom without haste and without effort, as a possession that is his own and that no one tries to wrest from him. *a

[Footnote a: The Americans, however, have not yet seen fit to strip the parent of one of the chief elements of parental authority, as has been done in France, by depriving him of the power to dispose of his property at his death. In the United States a testator’s powers have no restrictions. In this respect, as in almost all others, it is easy to see that although the political legislation of the Americans is much more democratic than that of the French, the civil legislation of the French is infinitely more democratic than that of the Americans. There is an easy explanation. The civil legislation of France was the work of a man who saw that it served his interest to satisfy the democratic passions of his contemporaries in everything that was not directly and immediately hostile to his own power. He was willing to let some popular principles govern the distribution of property and the government of families, so long as they were not brought into the administration of public affairs. While the torrent of democracy swept over the civil laws of the country, he hoped to find an easy shelter behind its political institutions. This policy was both adroit and selfish. But a compromise of this kind could not last, because in the end political institutions always become the image and expression of civil society. In this sense it can be said that nothing in a nation is more political than its civil legislation.]

It may be useful to show how these changes in family relations are closely tied to the social and political revolution that is nearing its completion before our eyes. There are certain great social principles that a people either introduces everywhere or tolerates nowhere. In countries organized on aristocratic lines, with all the gradations of rank, the government never appeals directly to the mass of the governed. Because men are bound together, it is enough to lead the foremost, and the rest will follow. The same holds for the family, as for every aristocracy that has a head. Among aristocratic nations, social institutions in truth recognize no one in the family but the father. Society receives the children from his hands; society governs him, and he governs them. So the parent has not only a natural right but also a political right to command them. He is the author and the support of his family, but he is also its appointed ruler. In democracies, the government singles out each individual from the mass to make him subject to the general laws of the community, and no such intermediary is needed. There, in the eyes of the law, a father is only a member of the community, older and richer than his sons.

When most of the conditions of life are extremely unequal, and that inequality is permanent, the idea of a superior takes a growing hold on people’s imaginations. If the law gave him no privileges, custom and public opinion would grant them. When, on the contrary, men differ little from one another and do not always remain in unlike conditions of life, the general idea of a superior grows weaker and less distinct. It is useless for legislation to try to set the one who obeys far beneath the one who commands; the customs of the time bring the two men closer together and draw them daily toward the same level. Suppose the legislation of an aristocratic people granted heads of families no particular privileges. I would be no less convinced that their power is more respected and more extensive than in a democracy, for I know that, whatever the laws may be, superiors always appear higher and inferiors lower in aristocracies than among democratic nations.

When men live more for the memory of what has been than for the care of what is, and when they are more inclined to attend to what their ancestors thought than to think for themselves, the father is the natural and necessary tie between the past and the present — the link joining the ends of these two chains. In aristocracies, then, the father is not only the civil head of the family but also the oracle of its traditions, the interpreter of its customs, and the arbiter of its mores. He is heard with deference and addressed with respect, and the love felt for him is always tempered with fear. When the condition of society becomes democratic, and men adopt as their general principle that it is good and lawful to judge all things for oneself — using earlier beliefs not as a rule of faith but simply as a source of information — the power of a father’s opinions over those of his sons shrinks, as his legal power does.

Perhaps nothing contributes more to changing the relations between a father and his children than the division of estates that democracy brings with it. When the father of a family has little property, he and his son live constantly in the same place and share the same occupations. Habit and necessity bring them together and force them into constant contact. The inevitable result is a kind of familiar intimacy, which makes authority less absolute and can hardly be reconciled with outward forms of respect. Now in democratic countries the class of those who hold small fortunes is precisely the class that gives strength to the ideas, and a particular direction to the mores, of the community. That class makes its opinions prevail as universally as its will, and even those most inclined to resist its commands are carried along in the end by its example. I have known eager opponents of democracy who let their children address them with perfect colloquial equality.

Thus, as the power of aristocracy declines, the austere, conventional and legal part of parental authority disappears, and a kind of equality prevails around the domestic hearth. I do not know whether society, on the whole, loses by the change, but I am inclined to believe that the individual gains by it. I think that as mores and laws become more democratic, the relation between father and son becomes more intimate and more affectionate. People speak less of rules and authority; confidence and tenderness often increase; and it seems that the natural bond tightens as the social bond loosens. In a democratic family the father exercises no power except what people love to give to the affection and experience of age. His orders might perhaps be disobeyed, but his advice is for the most part respected as authoritative. He is not hedged in by ceremonial respect, yet his sons at least approach him with confidence. No set form of speech is reserved for addressing him; they talk to him constantly and are ready to consult him day by day. The master and the appointed ruler have vanished; the father remains. To judge how the two states of society differ in this respect, one needs only to read the family correspondence of aristocratic ages. The style is always correct, ceremonious and stiff, and so cold that the natural warmth of the heart can hardly be felt in the language. The language a son addresses to his father in democratic countries, by contrast, always mixes freedom, familiarity and affection, which shows at once that new relations have sprung up within the family.

A similar revolution takes place in the relations of children to one another. In aristocratic families, as in aristocratic society, every place is marked out in advance. Not only does the father hold a separate rank, with extensive privileges, but even the children are not equal among themselves. Each child’s age and sex fix his rank irrevocably and secure him certain privileges. Democracy abolishes or reduces most of these distinctions. In aristocratic families the eldest son inherits the greater part of the property and almost all the rights of the family, and so becomes the chief, and to some extent the master, of his brothers. Greatness and power are for him; mediocrity and dependence are for them. Nevertheless, it would be wrong to suppose that among aristocratic nations the eldest son’s privileges benefit himself alone, or that they arouse only envy and hatred in those around him. The eldest son usually tries to win wealth and power for his brothers, because the general splendor of the house reflects back on the one who represents it. The younger sons try to support their elder brother in all his undertakings, because the greatness and power of the head of the family put him in a better position to provide for every branch. The members of an aristocratic family are therefore bound very closely together. Their interests are linked and their minds agree, but their hearts are seldom in harmony.

Democracy also binds brothers to one another, but by very different means. Under democratic laws all the children are perfectly equal, and therefore independent. Nothing forcibly brings them together, but nothing keeps them apart. They have the same origin, they are brought up under the same roof, they are treated with the same care, and no particular privilege distinguishes or divides them. So the affectionate, youthful intimacy of the early years easily grows up between them. Hardly any occasion arises to break the tie formed at the start of life, because their brotherhood brings them together every day without embarrassing them. It is not, then, by interest but by shared associations and by the free sympathy of opinion and taste that democracy unites brothers. It divides their inheritance, but it lets their hearts and minds mingle. Such is the charm of these democratic mores that even the partisans of aristocracy are won over by it. After experiencing it for some time, they are not at all tempted to go back to the respectful, frigid observance of aristocratic families. They would gladly keep the domestic habits of democracy if they could cast off its social conditions and its laws. But these elements are inseparably joined, and it is impossible to enjoy the former without putting up with the latter. What I have said about filial love and fraternal affection applies to all the passions that arise spontaneously from human nature itself. If a certain way of thinking or feeling results from some particular condition of life, then when that condition changes, nothing at all remains of the thought or feeling. A law may bind two members of the community very closely to each other, but once that law is abolished, they stand apart. Nothing was stricter than the tie that joined the vassal to the lord under the feudal system. Today the two men do not know each other. The fear, the gratitude and the affection that once connected them have vanished, and not a trace of the tie remains. This is not the case, however, with the feelings that are natural to mankind. Whenever a law tries to direct these feelings in a particular way, it nearly always weakens them. By trying to increase their intensity, it strips them of some of their elements, for they are never stronger than when left to themselves.

Democracy destroys or obscures almost all the old conventional rules of society, and it keeps men from readily accepting new ones. As a result, it entirely wipes out most of the feelings that those conventional rules gave rise to. Others it only modifies, and it often gives them a degree of energy and sweetness unknown before. Perhaps the whole meaning of this chapter, and of several earlier ones, can be condensed into a single proposition. Democracy loosens social ties but draws the ties of nature tighter; it brings kindred closer together while setting the various members of the community farther apart.
